"What?" Captain Sterling demanded, his eyes flashing from the static-filled radio set to the calm face of the young woman beside him. "What was that, Hanson?"

"The mission is scrubbed, sir," Lieutenant Hanson repeated, her voice steady. "Command's orders. We're to return to the rendezvous point immediately."

"Return to the point?" Sterling scoffed, running a hand through his sweat-dampened hair. "We're two hours from the objective! We finally have a clear window to get that intel. Did they give a reason?"

"No, sir," she replied. "Just the authentication code and the direct order. 'Mission Blackwood is terminated.' Those were the exact words."

"I don't like it," the captain said, tight-lipped, as he stared out the armored viewport of the crawler into the swirling Martian dust. "I don't like it one bit. We've been planning this for six months. Why pull the plug now? Unless--"

"Unless what, sir?" Hanson prompted when he fell silent.

For a moment the captain held his lips pressed together in a thin, grim line. He looked at the lieutenant, a new, hard light in his eyes. "Tell me, Hanson, you were top of your class in cryptology at the Academy, weren't you?"

"I was, sir," she confirmed, a slight frown creasing her brow. "Why do you ask?"

"That authentication code. Was there anything funny about it? Anything at all?"

The lieutenant's frown deepened. "Funny, sir? No. It was a standard Delta-class sequence. Perfectly valid." She paused, her gaze turning inward as she replayed the signal in her mind. "There was one thing, though. A slight delay in the seventh tonal pulse. Only a millisecond. Probably just atmospheric interference."

"No," Sterling said, his voice dropping to a near whisper. "There's no such thing as 'just interference' out here. The geniuses at Command wouldn't risk a miscommunication on a millisecond anomaly. That delay was intentional."

The horrible thought made Hanson's breath catch in her throat, and she thanked the stars that they hadn't simply followed the order blindly. To have turned back would have been bad enough, but to have done so without understanding the reason would have been a catastrophic failure.

"What does it mean, sir?" she asked after several moments of tense silence. "Is it some kind of warning?"

Captain Sterling didn't answer right away. He stared down at his gloved hands, which were clenched into tight fists on the console. The expression on his rugged face seemed to show a reluctance to give voice to the idea forming in his mind.

"It's a contingency," he began quietly. "One they briefed me on, and only me. I was ordered to never speak of it unless I was absolutely certain. That delay, Hanson... it's a signal. It means the intel we came for is a decoy. A plant."

"A plant, sir?" Hanson gasped. "But the source was verified! We sacrificed two scout teams confirming the location!"

"I know," the captain said, stopping her with a gesture of his hand. "But look at it this way. Suppose the enemy wanted us to retrieve that data? Suppose they let our scouts get just close enough to confirm the target, knowing we'd send in a primary recovery team? What then?"

"They'd be waiting for us, sir," Hanson said, the color draining from her face. "An ambush."

"Exactly," the captain agreed. "A perfect little trap, and we'd be driving right into it. But the decoy works both ways. Command planted that termination order with a specific tell, the one you just caught. They suspected the entire operation might be compromised from the start. They sent us out here not to retrieve their data, but to see if the enemy would try to stop us."

"So the 'return to base' order," Hanson said slowly, the truth hitting her like a physical blow. "If we had obeyed it, we would have confirmed to the enemy that we knew their data was a trap?"

"I mean just that!" the captain confirmed grimly. "Our retreat would have been the signal. It would tell them that we're aware of their counter-intelligence methods. They'd burn all their current assets and we'd lose years of work. Think of it! Our entire network of informants on Mars, gone in a puff of smoke!"

"So what's our move now, sir?" Hanson asked, her mind racing. "The ambush is still waiting for us at the objective."

"A good question, and I've got the answer." The captain smiled, a grim, wolfish expression. "The enemy wants us to think we're walking into their trap. So that's exactly what we'll do. We proceed as planned. We make it look like we never received the termination order, or that we missed the tell. We let them think we're fools."

"But, sir," Hanson protested, "we'll be annihilated! The crawler can't stand up to a full platoon of their heavy armor!"

"We won't have to," the captain said, and pointed to a small, locked case bolted beneath the console. "Command had a contingency for the contingency. They were hoping the enemy would take the bait. In there is a viral override. If we get within five hundred meters of their command post, I can upload it. It won't just neutralize the platoon waiting for us. It will cripple their entire sector command."

"Well," Hanson remarked, and checked the charge on her sidearm, "that's one way to change the odds--"

But she never finished her sentence, because at that moment a proximity alarm blared through the cockpit.

Another burst of cannon fire ripped the air, this time closer. The entire bomber vibrated violently, and the lights in their compartment flickered and died, plunging them into near total darkness, lit only by the faint moonlight filtering through the small window.

"He's right, sir!" Freddy chimed in, his voice sharp and eager. "This crate has teeth. Let us at them!"

"The waist guns are manned," the pilot's voice cut in again, "but the tail gunner isn't responding! I think he's hit!"

Dawson squinted against the wind, his eyes trying to adjust to the stark contrast of inky black sky and the brilliant, terrifying flashes of enemy tracers. He saw the two waist gunners, strapped into their positions, swinging their heavy machine guns, firing in short, controlled bursts.
He grabbed the shoulder of the port side gunner. "Dawson!" he yelled over the noise. "Colonel's orders! Let me take it!"
The gunner, a young sergeant with a look of intense concentration on his face, glanced back, his eyes wide. He recognized the famous ace instantly. Without a word, he unstrapped himself and squeezed past, giving Dawson room. "He's all yours, sir!" he shouted. "Give 'em hell!"

He slammed a fresh belt of ammunition into the feed tray, racked the charging handle, and swung the barrel out into the night.
For a moment, he was back in his Spitfire, the world reduced to a patch of sky and the enemy in his sights. He scanned the darkness, his trained eyes searching for the telltale flicker of an engine's exhaust, the sleek silhouette of a German killer.

The German plane kept coming, its own cannons still spitting fire. Dawson gritted his teeth, correcting his aim, fighting the bucking of the gun and the violent lurching of his own aircraft. Then he saw it. A flicker of orange, then a blossom of bright yellow flame from the Ju 88's engine nacelle.

"You've got him!" Freddy yelled from the other side. "He's smoking!"

The German pilot was a fighter, though. Instead of breaking off, he seemed to redouble his attack, trying to take them with him. A fresh hail of cannon shells tore along the B-25's wing, and a loud clang echoed from somewhere forward. Dawson ignored it, keeping his sights on the wounded enemy. The fire on the Ju 88's wing grew, trailing a thick plume of black smoke that was starkly visible against the moonlit clouds below. The bomber faltered, its nose dipping heavily. It slid sideways, out of its attack run, and began a long, spiraling plunge toward the dark, unforgiving waters of the Atlantic.

"Nice shooting, Dave!" Freddy's voice was a cheerful shout. "Just like old times, eh?"

"There's more!" a voice crackled over the intercom, the pilot's tone urgent and strained. "Two more! Starboard side, high!"

Dawson didn't have to look. Freddy's gun was already barking, its thunderous rhythm joining the chorus of the top turret and the tail gunner. Dawson swiveled his own gun, trying to get an angle, but the attackers were on the other side of the B-25. The pilot threw the big bomber into a sickening dive, pressing them all against the ceiling. Dawson's stomach lurched, and he braced himself against the fuselage wall.

"They're Focke-Wulfs!" the pilot's voice came again. "Long range fighters! They're coming around!"

As the B-25 leveled out, Dawson caught a glimpse of one of the German fighters. It was a Focke-Wulf 190, its sharklike profile unmistakable. It was faster and more agile than the Ju 88, a pure-bred killer. It flashed past them, tracers zipping through the space they had occupied a second before, then banked sharply to come around for another pass.

"Here comes the other one!" Freddy shouted a warning.

This time, the attack was on Dawson's side. The Focke-Wulf screamed in from ten o'clock, its nose lit up with the rapid fire of four cannons and two machine guns. Dawson met the attack with his own stream of fifty caliber slugs. It was like trying to hit a hornet with a rock. The fighter jinked and weaved, its tracers whipping past Dawson's head, so close he could feel their heat. One shell smashed into the Plexiglas of the waist gunner's window, which exploded inward, showering him with sharp fragments. He grunted in pain, feeling a sharp sting on his cheek, but he didn't let up. He kept firing, tracking the agile fighter with a grim determination.

He didn't hit it. The fighter was too fast, the pilot too skilled. It zoomed over them and climbed for altitude, ready to dive again.

"Colonel Welsh, sir!" the pilot's voice crackled, laced with worry. "We've taken hits in the starboard engine! Oil pressure is dropping fast!"

Dawson's heart sank. A crippled engine over the middle of the Atlantic at night, with two enemy fighters on their tail, was as close to a death sentence as you could get.

"Keep her flying, Lieutenant!" Colonel Welsh's voice came back, as calm and cold as ice. "Dawson, Farmer, can you keep them off us?"

"We're doing our best, sir!" Dawson yelled back into the wind. He swiped at his cheek, and his glove came away wet. He ignored it. He slammed the breech cover open and reached for a new ammunition belt, his movements sure and practiced despite the chaos. The young sergeant who had given up the gun was there, holding a fresh can ready.

"Here you go, sir!" the sergeant said, his voice steady. "Let me know if you need another!"

"Thanks!" Dawson grunted, feeding the belt into the gun. "Just stay down!"

He snapped the cover shut and charged the weapon. At the same moment, Freddy's gun fell silent.

"Dave! I'm jammed!" the English youth cried out in frustration. "The feed mechanism is shot to pieces!"

Dawson's blood ran cold. The top turret and tail guns were still firing, but without both waist guns, they had a massive blind spot. The German pilots would spot the weakness in a heartbeat.

"Get on the other side of me!" Dawson shouted. "Spot for me! Tell me where they are!"

Freddy scrambled across the heaving floor of the fuselage. "Right! One is coming down, Dave! A steep dive, right for our tail!"

The tail gunner's fifty calibers hammered away, and Dawson could see the tracers from the Focke-Wulf streaking toward the B-25's empennage. The pilot kicked the rudder, and the plane skewed sideways, trying to throw off the German's aim.

"The other one!" Freddy yelled in his ear, pointing out the shattered port window. "He's coming in low again! Your side! He's using his partner's attack as a screen!"

It was a classic tactic. One fighter draws your attention while the other sneaks in for the kill. Dawson swung the heavy barrel of the Browning around, his eyes straining in the dark. He saw him, a dark shape against a sliver of moonlight on the water. He was low, all right, and coming up fast.

"I've got him!" Dawson said, his voice a low growl. "I've got him."

This time he didn't wait. He didn't have the luxury of a perfect shot. He opened fire, sending a long, searching burst of tracers toward the spot where he knew the fighter had to be. He wasn't aiming for the plane itself, but for the air just in front of it. The German pilot would have to fly right through the storm of steel.

For a terrifying instant, the Focke-Wulf continued its charge, its own guns blazing. A line of explosive shells stitched a pattern across the B-25's belly. The deck beneath Dawson's feet jumped, and a new, high pitched shriek of tortured metal filled the air. But Dawson held his fire steady, his entire being focused on that one patch of night sky.

Then, his gamble paid off. His stream of tracers connected. Not with a flash and a fire, but with a sudden, violent swerve. The Focke-Wulf, mortally wounded, seemed to cartwheel. Its wing dipped, caught the air wrong, and the entire aircraft snapped into a vicious, uncontrolled spin. It vanished from sight, tumbling end over end toward the sea.

"You did it!" Freddy screamed, pounding him on the back. "You hit him! He's gone!"

The remaining Focke-Wulf, its partner suddenly gone, seemed to lose its nerve. After one more blistering pass at their tail, which was met with a furious return of fire from the tail gunner, it broke off the engagement. It waggled its wings in a final, defiant gesture and then climbed away, disappearing into the vast, lonely darkness of the east.

For a full minute, there was no sound in the waist section but the roar of their own engines, one of which was now making a horrible grinding noise, and the whistle of wind through the shattered window. Dawson slumped against the gun mount, his arms aching, the adrenaline slowly beginning to drain away.

"All stations, report!" Colonel Welsh's voice cut through the relative quiet.

"Tail gunner here, sir," a voice answered. "I'm okay. A few holes in the tail plane, but the controls feel responsive."

"Top turret, okay, sir," another voice said.

"Radio operator. We're fine back here, Colonel."

"Waist here, sir," Dawson said, his voice hoarse. He cleared his throat. "Farmer and I are all right. The port window is gone, and we have some new holes in the floor. Freddy's gun is out of action."

There was a pause. "And the starboard engine, Lieutenant?" the colonel asked the pilot.

The pilot's reply was grim. "It's gone, sir. I've feathered the prop. We're losing altitude. I don't know if we can hold this height on one engine, not with the extra fuel load we're carrying."

A heavy silence descended on the crew. Dawson looked at Freddy, whose face was pale in the dim light of the fuselage. The elation of their victory had evaporated, replaced by a cold, hard reality. They were hundreds of miles from land, in a crippled bomber, with the enemy now fully aware of their existence and their presumed cargo.

"We have to lighten the load," Colonel Welsh's voice came again, devoid of any emotion. "Jettison everything that isn't bolted down. Ammunition cans, loose equipment, personal gear. Everything. Dawson, you and Farmer supervise."

"Yes, sir," Dawson said automatically.

He and Freddy, joined by the two sergeants who had manned the guns, immediately set to work. They opened the bomb bay doors just enough to push out the heavy cans of fifty caliber ammunition, saving only a few belts for the remaining guns. Tool kits, spare parts, anything that had weight was ruthlessly shoved out into the night. They worked with a frantic, desperate energy. Every pound they shed was another few feet of altitude, another few seconds of life.

After ten minutes of furious labor, the plane was as bare as they could make it. Dawson made his way forward, stumbling as the plane shuddered, and squeezed into the cockpit. The scene was one of controlled chaos. The pilot and copilot were fighting the controls, their faces illuminated by the eerie red and green glow of the instrument panel. Colonel Welsh was wedged between them, his eyes fixed on the altimeter. It was still dropping, but much more slowly now.

"Are we going to make it, sir?" Dawson asked, his voice low.

The pilot answered without looking at him. "We've stopped the freefall, but we're still sinking. We're too heavy. The drag from the dead engine is killing us. We can't maintain altitude."

Colonel Welsh turned his head, and his eyes met Dawson's. In their depths, Dawson saw not fear, but a cold, hard calculation. The Chief of Intelligence was weighing odds, just as he always did.

"There is one more thing we can jettison," the colonel said quietly, his voice barely audible over the one laboring engine. "The extra fuel tanks. The ones in the bomb bay."

The pilot and copilot both turned to stare at him. "Sir," the pilot said, aghast. "If we do that, we'll never make Casablanca. We won't even make it back to the coast of Africa. We'll have to ditch in the ocean."

"I am aware of that, Lieutenant," Colonel Welsh replied evenly. "But it is better than crashing into the ocean. Ditching gives us a chance. A slim one, but a chance. Crashing gives us none." He looked at Dawson. "Your thoughts, Dawson? You've flown more combat missions than anyone here."

Dawson frowned, his mind racing. The colonel was right. If they couldn't hold altitude, they were doomed anyway. The information in the envelopes we destroyed stated that a substitute plane, a B-25, was taking a southern route. They have destroyed that plane. They now believe the route is clear. However, the information von Steuben may have stolen contained a third contingency: that in the event of the loss of both primary and secondary planes, a high speed, unmarked transport would make a direct dash for Casablanca. That is what they are looking for now. They will be watching the main shipping corridor. We are going to fly right into it."
"We're the bait again, sir?" Dawson asked.
"More than bait, Dawson," the colonel corrected. "We are the confirmation. When they see a single, high-speed American plane flying this route, they will be certain. They will throw everything they have at us to stop us from reaching Casablanca. And we will let them."
"Let them?" Freddy piped up. "Sir, I'm not sure I fancy that idea!"
"Your job is not to win a battle, Farmer," Welsh said, his voice hard as steel. "Your job is to spot them. Dawson's job is to fly the plane. My job is to make sure the real President lands safely in three hours. He is landing, gentlemen, because the entire German air command in this sector will be chasing us. Do you understand?"
The terrible, brilliant logic of the plan settled over Dawson. They were a ghost, a phantom chase designed to draw the hounds away from the real fox.
"I understand, sir," Dawson said grimly.
"Good. Then fly, Dawson. Fly like the devil himself is on your tail."
For an hour, there was nothing. Only the endless blue of the sky above and the ocean below, and the steady drone of the Allison engines. Dawson was slowly getting the feel of the powerful fighter. It was sensitive, responsive to the slightest touch, a true pilot's airplane.
"Bogey," Freddy's voice said, suddenly sharp and clear. "High, at two o'clock."
Dawson's head snapped up. He saw it then, a tiny black speck against the brilliant sky.
"He's seen us," Dawson said, his hand instinctively tightening on the control yoke. "He's changing course."
"What is it, Farmer?" the colonel's voice cut in.
"Looks like a Condor, sir. A Focke-Wulf 200. Long-range maritime patrol."
"The perfect scout," Welsh said. "He'll radio our position. Do not engage him, Dawson. Let him get a good, long look. Let him report back to his masters that he's found the prize."
It was the hardest order Dawson had ever had to follow. Every instinct screamed at him to climb, to attack, to wipe the snooping German plane from the sky. Instead, he held his course, flying straight and level, a perfect target.
The Condor shadowed them for ten agonizing minutes, staying just out of range. Dawson could practically feel the German radio operator's fingers tapping out the message that would seal their fate. Then, as suddenly as it had appeared, the German plane banked steeply and headed east, disappearing into the haze.
"He's gone to tell his friends," Freddy reported.
"Now the waiting begins," Colonel Welsh said. "Stay sharp."
They didn't have to wait long.
"Bandits!" Freddy yelled, his voice cracking with urgency. "Lots of them! Coming in from the east! Nine o'clock, level!"
Dawson's blood ran cold. He looked left and saw them. A swarm of angry black dots, growing larger by the second. They weren't Condors. They were fighters.
"Messerschmitts," Dawson spat, his knuckles white. "Looks like a whole squadron. At least twelve of them."
"This is it, boys," Colonel Welsh said, his voice eerily calm over the intercom. "This is what we came for. Make them believe it. Make them fight for it."
The German fighters split into two groups, one climbing high to come down on them from above, the other streaking in low and fast.
"Here they come!" Freddy shouted.
"I see them!" Dawson snapped. He flicked the gun arming switches. A row of green lights glowed on his panel. He pushed the throttles to the fire wall, and the P-38 surged forward, the engines screaming.
"First group, from the left!" Freddy called.
Dawson rolled the Lightning hard to the left, standing it on a wingtip. A stream of cannon shells stitched a line across the sky exactly where they had been a second before. He hauled back on the yoke, climbing into a steep, spiraling ascent. The G-force pressed him deep into his seat. He glanced back and saw two Bf 109s climbing after him, their yellow noses stark against the blue.
"They're on our tail, Dave!"
"I know!" Dawson grunted. He pushed the yoke forward, nosing the P-38 into a terrifying dive. The Messerschmitts, not as strong in a dive, struggled to follow. The air speed indicator needle raced around the dial. The plane shrieked in protest. He pulled out at the last second, leveling off just above the waves, the tips of the props seeming to kiss the tops of the swells.
"Where are they?" he gasped, his eyes scanning the mirrors.
"They overshot! Coming around for another pass!" Freddy said. "The high group is starting its dive!"
It was a classic pincer movement. Dawson was trapped. He could either face the two on his tail or the half dozen diving on him from the sun.
"Dawson," the colonel's voice said, steady as a rock. "Your primary objective is Casablanca. Do not get drawn into a turning fight. Use your speed. Run if you have to."
But Dawson knew running wasn't an option. They were too many, and they had him boxed in. A cold fury rose in him. They had killed the B-25 pilot. They had hunted them across the ocean. They thought he was a helpless transport. It was time to show them what the fork-tailed devil could do.
"Freddy," Dawson said, his voice low and dangerous. "Pick me a target."
A split second of silence. Then, "Lead plane. High group. The one with the fancy paint job."
Dawson smiled, a grim, tight slash of a smile. "I see him."
He rolled the Lightning onto its back and pulled, looping up and into the path of the diving Germans. It was a maneuver of pure, suicidal audacity. For a moment, he was flying head on into the entire enemy squadron. His thumb found the firing stud.
The nose of the P-38 erupted in a torrent of fire and thunder, the four fifty caliber machine guns and the twenty millimeter cannon all speaking at once. The lead Messerschmitt, its pilot no doubt frozen in disbelief, flew directly into the wall of lead. The plane didn't just explode. It vaporized, disintegrating into a cloud of black smoke and tiny, glittering fragments.
Dawson jinked hard right, and the sky around him was filled with the angry hornet-buzz of cannon shells. The chase was on.
